{{Short description|Theorem in queueing theory}}
In mathematical [[queueing theory]], '''Little's law''' (also '''result''', '''theorem''', '''lemma''', or '''formula'''<ref>{{cite book|title=Probability, statistics, and random processes for electrical engineering|author=Alberto Leon-Garcia|publisher=Prentice Hall|year=2008|edition=3rd|isbn=978-0-13-147122-1}}</ref><ref name="allen">{{cite book | page = [https://archive.org/details/probabilitystati0000alle/page/259 259] | title = Probability, Statistics, and Queueing Theory: With Computer Science Applications | first = Arnold A. | last = Allen | publisher = Gulf Professional Publishing | year = 1990 | isbn = 0120510510 | url = https://archive.org/details/probabilitystati0000alle/page/259 }}</ref>) is a theorem by [[John Little (academic)|John Little]] which states that the long-term average number of customers (''L'') in a [[stationary process|stationary]] system is equal to the long-term average effective arrival rate (''&lambda;'') multiplied by the average time that a customer spends in the system (''W''). Expressed algebraically the law is

: <math> L = \lambda W. </math>

The relationship is not influenced by the arrival process distribution, the service distribution, the service order, or practically anything else. In most queuing systems, service time is the [[Bottleneck (engineering)|bottleneck]] that creates the queue.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Simchi-Levi | first1 = D. | last2 = Trick | first2 = M. A.|author2-link= Michael Trick | doi = 10.1287/opre.1110.0941 | title = Introduction to "Little's Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary" | journal = Operations Research | volume = 59 | issue = 3 | pages = 535 | year = 2013}}</ref>

The result applies to any system, and particularly, it applies to systems within systems.<ref>{{Cite book | last1 = Serfozo | first1 = R. | chapter = Little Laws | doi = 10.1007/978-1-4612-1482-3_5 | title = Introduction to Stochastic Networks | pages = 135–154 | year = 1999 | isbn = 978-1-4612-7160-4 }}</ref> For example in a bank branch, the [[queue area|customer line]] might be one subsystem, and each of the [[Bank teller|tellers]] another subsystem, and Little's result could be applied to each one, as well as the whole thing. The only requirement is that the system be [[Ergodicity|ergodic]].<ref>{{Cite book | last=Harchol-Balter | first=Mor | chapter = Chapter 6: Little's Law and Other Operational Laws | title=Performance Modeling and Design of Computer Systems: Queueing Theory in Action | publisher=Cambridge University Press | page=98}}</ref>

In some cases it is possible not only to mathematically relate  the ''average'' number in the system to the ''average'' wait but even to relate the entire ''[[probability distribution]]'' (and moments) of the number in the system to the wait.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Keilson | first1 = J. | author-link1 = Julian Keilson| last2 = Servi | first2 = L. D. | doi = 10.1016/0167-6377(88)90035-1 | title = A distributional form of Little's Law | journal = Operations Research Letters | volume = 7 | issue = 5 | pages = 223 | year = 1988 | hdl = 1721.1/5305 | url = https://dspace.mit.edu/bitstream/1721.1/47244/1/distributionalfo00keil.pdf | hdl-access = free }}</ref>

==History==

In a 1954 paper, Little's law was assumed true and used without proof.<ref name="little-graves">{{Cite book | last1 = Little | first1 = J. D. C. | author-link1=John Little (academic)| last2 = Graves | first2 = S. C. | chapter = Little's Law | doi = 10.1007/978-0-387-73699-0_5 | title = Building Intuition | series = International Series in Operations Research & Management Science | volume = 115 | pages = 81 | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-0-387-73698-3 | chapter-url = http://web.mit.edu/sgraves/www/papers/Little's%20Law-Published.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Cobham | first1 = Alan| doi = 10.1287/opre.2.1.70 | title = Priority Assignment in Waiting Line Problems | journal = Operations Research | volume = 2 | issue = 1| pages = 70–76 | year = 1954 | jstor = 166539}}</ref> The form ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''λW'' was first published by [[Philip M. Morse]] where he challenged readers to find a situation where the relationship did not hold.<ref name="little-graves" /><ref>{{cite book | title = Queues, inventories, and maintenance: the analysis of operational system with variable demand and supply | first = Philip M. | last = Morse | author-link = Philip M. Morse | publisher= Wiley | year = 1958 | quote = "Those readers who would like to experience for themselves the slipperiness of fundamental concepts in this field and the intractability of really general theorems, might try their hand at showing under what circumstances this simple relationship between L and W does not hold." }}</ref> Little published  in 1961 his proof of the law, showing that no such situation existed.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Little | first1 = J. D. C. | author-link = John Little (academic)| title = A Proof for the Queuing Formula: ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''λW'' | doi = 10.1287/opre.9.3.383 | journal = [[Operations Research (journal)|Operations Research]]| volume = 9 | issue = 3 | pages = 383–387 | year = 1961 | jstor = 167570}}</ref> Little's proof was followed by a simpler version by Jewell<ref>{{cite journal | first = William S. | last = Jewell | year = 1967 | title = A Simple Proof of: ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''λW'' | journal = Operations Research | volume = 15 | issue = 6 | pages = 1109–1116 | jstor = 168616 | doi = 10.1287/opre.15.6.1109 }}</ref> and another by Eilon.<ref>{{cite journal | first= Samuel | last = Eilon | year = 1969 | title = A Simpler Proof of ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''λW'' | journal = Operations Research | volume = 17 | issue = 5 | pages = 915–917 | jstor = 168368 | doi = 10.1287/opre.17.5.915 | doi-access = free }}</ref> Shaler Stidham published a different and more intuitive proof in 1972.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Stidham Jr. | first1 = Shaler| title = A Last Word on ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''λW'' | doi = 10.1287/opre.22.2.417 | journal = Operations Research | volume = 22 | issue = 2 | pages = 417–421 | year = 1974 | jstor = 169601| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Stidham Jr. | first1 = Shaler| title = ''L''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''λW'': A Discounted Analogue and a New Proof | doi = 10.1287/opre.20.6.1115 | jstor = 169301| journal = Operations Research | volume = 20 | issue = 6 | pages = 1115–1120 | year = 1972 }}</ref>

==Examples==
{{More citations needed|section|date=December 2025}}
=== Finding response time ===

Imagine an application that had no easy way to measure [[Response time (technology)|response time]]. If the mean number in the system and the throughput are known, the average response time can be found using Little’s Law:

:: mean response time = mean number in system / mean throughput

For example: A queue depth meter shows an average of nine jobs waiting to be serviced. Add one for the job being serviced, so there is an average of ten jobs in the system. Another meter shows a mean throughput of 50 per second. The mean response time is calculated as 0.2 seconds = 10 / 50 per second.

=== Customers in the store ===

Imagine a small store with a single counter and an area for browsing, where only one person can be at the counter at a time, and no one leaves without buying something.  So the system is:

::''entrance → browsing → counter → exit''

If the rate at which people enter the store (called the arrival rate) is the rate at which they exit (called the exit rate), the system is stable.  By contrast, an arrival rate exceeding an exit rate would represent an unstable system, where the number of waiting customers in the store would gradually increase towards infinity.

Little's Law tells us that the average number of customers in the store ''L'', is the effective arrival rate&nbsp;''λ'', times the average time that a customer spends in the store ''W'', or simply:

: <math>L = \lambda  W </math>

Assume customers arrive at the rate of 10 per hour and stay an average of 0.5 hour.  This means we should find the average number of customers in the store at any time to be&nbsp;5.
: <math>L = 10 \times 0.5 = 5 </math>

Now suppose the store is considering doing more advertising to raise the arrival rate to 20 per hour.  The store must either be prepared to host an average of 10 occupants or must reduce the time each customer spends in the store to 0.25 hour.  The store might achieve the latter by ringing up the bill faster or by adding more counters.

We can apply Little's Law to systems within the store.  For example, consider the counter and its queue.  Assume we notice that there are on average 2 customers in the queue and at the counter.  We know the arrival rate is 10 per hour, so customers must be spending 0.2 hours on average checking out.
: <math>W =\frac{L}{\lambda} = \frac{2}{10} = 0.2 </math>

We can even apply Little's Law to the counter itself.  The average number of people at the counter would be in the range (0,&nbsp;1) since no more than one person can be at the counter at a time.  In that case, the average number of people at the counter is also known as the utilisation of the counter.

However, because a store in reality generally has a limited amount of space, it can eventually become unstable. If the arrival rate is much greater than the exit rate, the store will eventually start to overflow, and thus any new arriving customers will simply be rejected (and forced to go somewhere else or try again later) until there is once again free space available in the store. This is also the difference between the ''arrival rate'' and the ''effective arrival rate'', where the arrival rate roughly corresponds to the rate at which customers arrive at the store, whereas the effective arrival rate corresponds to the rate at which customers ''enter'' the store. However, in a system with an infinite size and no loss, the two are equal.

==Estimating parameters==

To use Little's law on data, formulas must be used to estimate the parameters, as the result does not necessarily directly apply over finite time intervals, due to problems like how to log customers already present at the start of the logging interval and those who have not yet departed when logging stops.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kim | first1 = S. H. | last2 = Whitt | first2 = W. | author-link2 = Ward Whitt| doi = 10.1287/opre.2013.1193 | title = Statistical Analysis with Little's Law | journal = Operations Research | volume = 61 | issue = 4 | pages = 1030 | year = 2013 | url = http://www.columbia.edu/~ww2040/LL_OR.pdf}}</ref>

==Applications==
Little's law is widely used in manufacturing to predict lead time based on the production rate and the amount of work-in-process.<ref>{{cite web | url= https://thesevendeadlywastes.com/lesson/lead-time/ | title = Manufacturing Lead Time | first = Nikolaus | last = Correll | date=June 13, 2021 | access-date = June 12, 2021}}</ref>

Software-performance testers have used Little's law to ensure that the observed performance results are not due to bottlenecks imposed by the testing apparatus.<ref>[http://www.onjava.com/pub/a/onjava/2005/01/19/j2ee-bottlenecks.html Software Infrastructure Bottlenecks in J2EE by Deepak Goel]</ref><ref>[https://arxiv.org/abs/cs/0404043 Benchmarking Blunders and Things That Go Bump in the Night by Neil Gunther]</ref>

Other applications include staffing emergency departments in hospitals.<ref name="50aniv">{{Cite journal | last1 = Little | first1 = J. D. C. | author-link = John Little (academic)| url = http://www.informs.org/content/download/255808/2414681/file/little_paper.pdf| title = Little's Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary | doi = 10.1287/opre.1110.0940 | journal = Operations Research | volume = 59 | issue = 3 | pages = 536–549 | year = 2011 | jstor = 23013126}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = http://www.epmonthly.com/subspecialties/management/littles-law-the-science-behind-proper-staffing/ | title = Little's Law: The Science Behind Proper Staffing | first = Mark | last = Harris | date = February 22, 2010 | access-date = September 4, 2012 | publisher = Emergency Physicians Monthly | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120905100132/http://www.epmonthly.com/subspecialties/management/littles-law-the-science-behind-proper-staffing/ | archive-date = September 5, 2012 | url-status = dead }}</ref>

Lastly, an equivalent version of Little's law also applies in the fields of [[demography]] and [[population biology]], although not referred to as "Little's Law".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Liang |first1=Haili |last2=Guo |first2=Zhen |last3=Tuljapurkar |first3=Shripad |date=2023 |title=Why life expectancy over-predicts crude death rate |journal=Genus |volume=79 |issue=1 |pages=9 |doi=10.1186/s41118-023-00188-8 |issn=2035-5556 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Murray |first=Bertram G. |date=2003 |title=A new equation relating population size and demographic parameters: some ecological implications |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/23736503 |journal=Annales Zoologici Fennici |volume=40 |issue=6 |pages=465–472 |jstor=23736503 |issn=0003-455X}}</ref> For example, Cohen (2008)<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=Joel E. |date=2008 |title=Constant global population with demographic heterogeneity |url=https://www.demographic-research.org/articles/volume/18/14 |journal=Demographic Research |language=en |volume=18 |pages=409–436 |doi=10.4054/DemRes.2008.18.14 |issn=1435-9871|doi-access=free }}</ref> explains that in a homogeneous stationary population without migration, <math> P = B \times e </math>, where <math> P </math> is the total population size, <math> B </math> is the number of births per year, and <math> e </math> is the life expectancy from birth. The formula <math> P = B \times e </math> is thus directly equivalent to Little's law (<math> L = \lambda \times W </math>). However, biological populations tend to be dynamic and therefore more complicated to model accurately.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Caswell |first=Hal |url=https://global.oup.com/academic/product/matrix-population-models-9780878931217 |title=Matrix population models: construction, analysis, and interpretation |date=2006 |publisher=Sinauer Associates, Inc. Publishers |isbn=978-0-87893-121-7 |edition=Second |location=Sunderland, Massachusetts}}</ref>

==Distributional form==

In some cases, it is possible not only to relate averages but to relate the entire probability distribution of the number in the system to the time in the system under a [[first come, first served]] discipline. A distributional relation for many FIFO/Poisson-class systems was derived by Keilson and Servi (1988)<ref name="KS88">{{cite journal |last1=Keilson |first1=Julian |last2=Servi |first2=Leslie D. |year=1988 |title=A distributional form of Little’s law |journal=Operations Research Letters |volume=7 |issue=5 |pages=223–227 |doi=10.1016/0167-6377(88)90035-1|hdl=1721.1/47244 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> and further developed in related work, including links to the Fuhrmann–Cooper decomposition<ref name="KS90">{{cite journal |last1=Keilson |first1=Julian |last2=Servi |first2=Leslie D. |year=1990 |title=The distributional form of Little's law and the Fuhrmann-Cooper decomposition |journal=Operations Research Letters |volume=9 |issue=4 |pages=239–247 |doi=10.1016/0167-6377(90)90068-G|hdl=1721.1/47195 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>; later, Bertsimas and Nakazato (1995) provided a new proof and surveyed applications.<ref>{{Cite journal | doi = 10.1287/opre.43.2.298| title = The Distributional Little's Law and Its Applications| journal = [[Operations Research (journal)|Operations Research]]| volume = 43| issue = 2| pages = 298| year = 1995| last1 = Bertsimas | first1 = D. | last2 = Nakazato | first2 = D. | url = http://web.mit.edu/dbertsim/www/papers/Queuing%20Theory/The%20distributional%20Little's%20law%20and%20its%20applications.pdf| jstor = 171838}}</ref>
